clue.text: Geo, for a golden example

parts.note: Geo is the first half of George, the name of several British kings, so the abbreviation is literally half of a monarch's name; the old gold coin worth ten shillings fits the golden example

explanation.surface: A note explaining that the abbreviation Geo serves as an illustration of something golden.
explanation.walkthrough: GEO is half of GEORGE, a sovereign's name; a HALF-SOVEREIGN was also a British gold coin worth ten shillings, hence 'a golden example'.
explanation.definitionFit: The half-sovereign was a small British gold coin, often stamped with a King George's head.

clue.text: Am I to suppose hire-purchase arrangement covers. ', river horses?

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things in a new order, so the letters of the phrase are reordered

parts.note: HP is the standard British abbreviation for hire-purchase, buying on instalments

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a hire-purchase deal would cover the cost of some river animals.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'covers' and the stray punctuation after it look like a printing fault and play no part. Hire-purchase is the British name for buying on instalments, which is why the surface speaks of covering a cost.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name for the animal means literally horse of the river.

clue.text: Blossom gets a diamond on account

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on top of another comes first

parts.note: Diamond Lil was the famous Mae West stage and film character, so a diamond is a Lil

explanation.surface: A woman receives a diamond bought on credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a diamond' suggests a gem, but it is the name Lil, from Mae West's character Diamond Lil.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilac is a shrub known for its fragrant purple or white flower clusters.

clue.text: Member of the pack gives grim scream

indicators.note: something that gives yields or bends out of shape, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rugby forward lets out a ferocious yell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pack' is the group of forwards in rugby, who form the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A rugby forward takes part in the scrimmage, the old word for a scrum.

clue.text: Sybil and Vi, made up rather obviously

indicators.note: made up means put together or reconstituted, so the two names are reassembled

explanation.surface: Two women, Sybil and Vi, wearing heavy make-up that is plain for all to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in plain sight means doing it in a way anyone can see.

clue.text: Recoil from Cockney sort of setter

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker of London traditionally drops the H at the start of a word

parts.note: a red setter is a kind of hunting dog, hence a red hound

explanation.surface: Someone flinches away from a London dog of the setter breed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' looks like a crossword compiler, but it is the dog; a Cockney says 'red 'ound'. Cockneys are working-class Londoners.
explanation.definitionFit: To redound in its older sense is to rebound or come back upon someone.

clue.text: Fighters, one on either side of the redcap

indicators.note: one thing sitting on another at its edges here wraps the middle piece between copies
a letter on either side means two copies, one at each end

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
a redcap is a British military policeman, abbreviated MP

explanation.surface: Soldiers flank a military policeman, one at each side.
explanation.walkthrough: A redcap is British army slang for a military policeman (MP), from the red cap cover.
explanation.definitionFit: An impi was a Zulu regiment of warriors.

clue.text: Lionesses, making no sound

indicators.note: making means forming or turning into, so the letters of the word are turned into a new word

explanation.surface: A pride of big cats moving silently.
explanation.definitionFit: Without any sound means completely silent.

clue.text: Trash collectors, Iago called them

parts.note: in Othello Iago says 'Who steals my purse steals trash', so thieves of money bags are collectors of trash in his terms

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's villain describing dustmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests refuse collectors, but Iago's line in Othello equates a purse with trash.
explanation.definitionFit: Street thieves who grab handbags take what Iago dismissed as trash.

clue.text: Star journalist went to extremes

parts.note: Polaris is the Pole Star
ED, short for editor, is a stock crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A celebrated reporter behaved immoderately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star journalist' reads as a top reporter; it splits into the Pole Star and an editor.
explanation.definitionFit: To be polarised is to be pushed to opposite poles or extremes.

clue.text: Tommy French

parts.note: Tommy is the nickname of the British private soldier; this asks for his French counterpart

explanation.surface: A man called Tommy French.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Atkins was the nickname of the ordinary British soldier; in the First World War his French opposite was the hairy one.
explanation.definitionFit: A poilu was a French infantry soldier of the First World War.

clue.text: There is a manly ring about this place of William's

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the sounded word is read backwards
a ring is a sound, as in a name with a familiar ring, so the word is taken by how it is heard

parts.note: macho means aggressively manly

explanation.surface: A place associated with a man named William has a masculine air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' is the sound-alike signal: MACCO sounds like MACHO, and 'about' turns MACCO round. William of Occam (Ockham) was the medieval philosopher of the razor.
explanation.definitionFit: The philosopher William of Ockham took his name from his birthplace, a village in Surrey.

clue.text: Athlete with cold?

definitions.meaning: at Oxford or Cambridge a sportsman who represents the university is awarded his colours
skin turns this shade when chilled

explanation.surface: A sportsman who has caught a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is an Oxford or Cambridge university sportsman or sportswoman.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxbridge sportsmen win colours named for a shade; freezing skin takes the same shade.

clue.text: Flower stands

definitions.meaning: crossword 'flower' is something that flows, a river; a river in north-east England
golfers rest the ball on small pegs before driving

explanation.surface: Displays for blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword river (one that flows): the Tees in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A river of northern England, and golf pegs supporting a ball.

clue.text: Over-provision of fruit

parts.note: an abundance of produce, the image of the overflowing goat's horn of classical myth

explanation.surface: Too much fruit has been supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: The horn of plenty, heaped with produce, stands for abundance.

clue.text: Where my bones may be put, as yours could be

definitions.text: Where my bones may be put

indicators.note: could be means might turn into, so the letters can be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone muses on where their remains might rest, adding that yours might go there too.
explanation.definitionFit: A charnel house or urn is a container for the skeletons of the dead.

clue.text: Second names — Eric had one

parts.note: a second title after the main one; Farrar's Victorian school story Eric carries one, 'Little by Little'

explanation.surface: Middle names, and a man called Eric had one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second names' suggests middle names, but these are second titles; F W Farrar's novel 'Eric, or, Little by Little' is the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A secondary title added after a book's main title gives it an alternative name.

clue.text: They, go to market for Dr Bowling

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, taken as printed
in cricket the bowling is delivered in overs of six balls

explanation.surface: People heading to market on behalf of a doctor named Bowling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowling' looks like a surname; it is cricket, where bowling comes in OVERS. The comma after 'They' is a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Herdsmen drive cattle or sheep to sell at the market.

clue.text: Egocentric, self-confessed crook is going around

indicators.note: ego is I, and centric puts it in the centre, so the I is moved to the middle

parts.note: a crook confessing would say 'I am bent', bent being slang for dishonest

explanation.surface: A selfish man who admits being dishonest is on the loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egocentric' looks like a character trait but it says put the ego (I) in the centre: I AM BENT becomes AM B-I-ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambient air or sound surrounds you on every side.

clue.text: Old net man's forked attacker

parts.note: the Roman retiarius gladiator fought with a net and a three-pronged spear

explanation.surface: A forked weapon used by an ancient fighter who carried a net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'net man' suggests a tennis player or fisherman, but this is the Roman gladiator who fought with net and spear.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-pronged spear, carried by the net-fighting gladiator.

clue.text: Admiral who corresponded with a Dean

definitions.meaning: the Red Admiral butterfly belongs to a genus with this name
Jonathan Swift, Dean of St Patrick's, wrote to Esther Vanhomrigh under this name

explanation.surface: A naval officer who exchanged letters with a cathedral dean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admiral' is the butterfly, not a naval officer; Swift's correspondent took the name he coined for her.
explanation.definitionFit: The butterfly genus of the Red Admiral, and Swift's nickname for his correspondent Esther Vanhomrigh.

clue.text: One who leaves his card, or comes after a call

indicators.note: one word coming after another means it is placed behind it

parts.note: to pay a call is to make a visit

explanation.surface: Someone who drops off a calling card, or arrives following a phone call.
explanation.walkthrough: In Victorian etiquette a caller left a visiting card.
explanation.definitionFit: A caller at a house would leave a calling card to show they had come.

clue.text: One expelled from a community

indicators.note: something expelled from a word is pushed out of it, so the letters are taken out of the inside

explanation.surface: A person thrown out of a community.
explanation.definitionFit: A single thing counted as a whole is a single entity.

clue.text: Is this denied or given by one crossed in love?

definitions.text: Is this denied or given by one crossed in love?

parts.words: Is this denied or given by one crossed in love?
parts.note: a lover thwarted may refuse an embrace of the lips, while a cross, X, is also the written sign for one

explanation.surface: A question about what a thwarted lover withholds or offers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossed in love' means thwarted, but a cross X is also written as this token at the end of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A touch of the lips, withheld in a quarrel or bestowed in love, and written as X.

clue.text: Akela, with the power of three?

definitions.text: Akela, with the power of three?

parts.words: Akela, with the power of three?
parts.note: Akela is the leader of a Cub Scout pack, and a quantity to the power of three is cubed

explanation.surface: A Cub Scout leader with triple authority.
explanation.walkthrough: Akela leads the Cubs; the clue reads 'Cub-ic', and power of three means cubed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cubic quantity is raised to the third power.

clue.text: Run onto the sands

explanation.surface: Someone dashing down to the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive a vessel onto the shore, and the sandy seashore itself.

clue.text: A threat to Sicilians to put up the stake

indicators.note: in a down clue putting up a word reads it from bottom to top

parts.note: the ante is the stake put in before a poker hand

explanation.surface: Sicilians face menace if they raise the stakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up the stake' sounds like raising a bet; in a down clue it turns ANTE upward.
explanation.definitionFit: The volcano of Sicily has erupted repeatedly and endangers nearby towns.

clue.text: Point about mica gets applause

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: talc is a soft mineral closely related to mica

explanation.surface: Making a point about a mineral earns a round of clapping.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat means brilliant success or acclaim.

clue.text: Bar torn from Pope's gate

indicators.note: torn means ripped apart, so the letters come from breaking up these words

parts.note: the possessive 's is used for its S letter here

explanation.surface: A barrier ripped from the Pope's gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a physical barrier; here it is the legal bar, an estoppage that stops a claim.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an estoppage is a bar preventing someone from denying an earlier statement.

clue.text: They keep legs clean by having sprints after a splash

indicators.note: one piece placed after another comes behind it

parts.note: a spatter is a splash of liquid
dashes are short fast runs

explanation.surface: Something keeps a runner's legs clean when he sprints through a splash.
explanation.definitionFit: Long gaiters once worn to protect stockings and trousers from mud.
